newsitem.title: USA: Begging for Gonzo, Thompson is fearless in New York.
newsitem.headline: Begging for Gonzo, Thompson is fearless in New York.

text.p: There is no gunfire or knife-throwing in Hunter S. Thompson's hotel room, but nearly every pore of your body warns you that there could be.

Thirty-one floors above Manhattan, ensconced in the marbled Four Seasons Hotel, Thompson proudly greets visitors, allowing strangers into the thousand miles of chaos that makes his life different from most others.
"Would you care for anything ... cigarette, marijuana?" he asks.

He sits, bathrobed, warm and lucid, ready for the story to unfold around him, securely hanging onto a tall glass of Chivas Regal. Open magazines and newspapers are scattered among various instruments of fun such as toy tomahawks and hammers amid the general clutter. A circle of supporters, his editor, friend and public relations handler, maintain order.

Thompson, 60, almost demure and entirely thoughtful as he is interviewed, appears to hold back nothing as he rages at his immediate enemies -- the hotel and its billing system. The dire threats lobbed in earlier times at the likes of Richard Nixon are now aimed at more pedestrian targets.

"When I came here they treated me not like the oil minister of Qatar (another hotel guest) but like some bum who wandered in off the street ... this is just a nasty dispute I'll grind in their f---ing throats," Thompson said.
ROAD MAN FOR THE LORDS OF KARMA

For four decades the man who has called himself a road man for the lords of karma has exploded the boundaries separating journalism and fiction, producing nine books and hundreds of articles, becoming the "gonzo" journalist for the ages.

Gonzo refers to a style of writing practiced by Thompson, requiring virtually no re-writing and based on aggressivly subjective reporting. "I just picked up gonzo as a term. I didn't think I was going to go on all alone into a different (journalistic) area," he said.

His style has also produced some of the finest political and social writing of his time, changing forever the relationship between author and subject in the 1960's with his inside look at the Hell's Angels motorcycle gang in California and in the early 1970's with "Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas" and "Fear and Loathing: On the Campaign Trail '72."

Thompson left his famous "armed compound" in the Colorado mountains to visit New York and push a newly published collection of his letters, "The Fear and Loathing Letters, Volume I: The Proud Highway, Saga of a Desperate Southern Gentleman" (Villard).

They are the first in a planned three-volume collection culled by University of New Orleans political science professor Douglas Brinkley, who uncovered more than 20,000 Thompson letters in the writer's Woody Creek, Colorado home.

Later volumes will track the even meatier years Thompson spent chronicling civil rights, Bobby Kennedy, political campaign trails, the drugging of American "new journalism," candidate Richard Nixon, and his own personal travails as a candidate for sheriff, an outlaw and a literary rock star.
SAVING ALL OF HIS LETTER
Thompson has said he carbon copied his own letters from teenage years on, all with the notion that someday the world would seek them out.
"Most of the letters are written to friends," he said. "It seemed to be a more articulate time. Other people were writing, too, it's just that I saved every one of them."
Before he was published, or even gainfully employed, the letters show Thompson telling Norman Mailer to shape up his writing and advising President Lyndon Johnson on Vietnam.

On the day President John Kennedy died, Nov. 22, 1963, Thompson set in motion -- through a letter to friend and author William Kennedy -- his fear and loathing creed. "No matter what, today is the end of an era. No more fair play. From now on it is dirty pool and judo in the clinches. The savage nuts have shattered the great myth of American decency. They can count me in -- I feel ready for a dirty game."

"(T)his is a very raw account of not just what it is like to be a freelance writer but also a journalist ... ever try to write fiction and be a reporter at the same time, novel in the lower desk drawer..." he replied when asked what the letters mean, trailing off into a sort of stream of consciousness.

The first volume of letters starts in 1955 and ends in 1967, a time span that saw Thompson leave his home in Louisville, straight from a jail cell for a robbery he said he did not commit, for a two-year stint in the Air Force. Keeping track of his post-military days tests the imagination.

He made stops and escapes from locales spanning the Caribbean to New York City and again to South America and back to the American West. Everywhere was considered, and every journalistic and literary outlet explored, all for the end of making it big.
Instead, he became gonzo -- mixing fact and fiction, taking readers on rides that could not quite be real.

"Nobody says that fiction has to be made up. Matter of fact, usually what it is is fairy tales ... another way of looking at what's going on. If you fictionalized your life and sell it, would it make any difference?" Thompson asks. "Would you be a different person?"
